Distributions
What makes Ubuntu and Fedora different distributions even though both use the Linux kernel?
They package different software, defaults, release cycles and package managers around the kernel
They each use a completely different kernel that is not related to Linux at all
Ubuntu is a desktop environment and Fedora is a command-line interpreter
Ubuntu runs only on servers and Fedora runs only on laptops and desktops
A distribution combines the kernel with userland tools, packaging and policies. Debian-family systems use apt/dpkg; Red Hat-family systems use dnf/rpm.
m
Identifying a system
Which file is the standard place to identify a Linux distribution and its version?
/etc/os-release
/etc/passwd
/var/log/syslog
/proc/cpuinfo
/etc/os-release holds the distribution name and version. /proc/cpuinfo describes the processor, not the distribution.
d
Release models
Why do many organisations prefer long-term-support (LTS) releases for servers?
They receive security updates for years without disruptive feature changes
They include the newest kernel features as soon as they are released upstream
They need no patching at all during their supported lifetime
They are the only releases that can be installed on virtual machines
LTS releases trade novelty for stability and a long security-support window, which suits production systems.
m
Shell basics
What is the relationship between a terminal and a shell?
The terminal displays input and output; the shell interprets the commands typed into it
The terminal interprets commands; the shell is only the window that displays text
They are two names for the same program on every Linux distribution
The shell is a hardware device and the terminal is its device driver
The terminal (emulator) handles display; the shell, such as bash, parses and runs commands.
d
Shell processing order
In bash, why does echo $HOME/*.txt list files rather than print a literal asterisk when matches exist?
The shell expands the variable and then the glob before the command runs
echo itself searches the directory for files that match the pattern
The kernel expands wildcards when the process opens its arguments
Globbing happens only when the pattern is inside double quotes
Expansion is done by the shell: parameter expansion, then pathname expansion. echo only receives the resulting words.
d
Quoting
A filename contains a space: 'Q1 report.txt'. Why does rm $f fail when f holds that name, while rm "$f" works?
Unquoted, the value is split into two words; double quotes keep it as one argument
Unquoted variables are ignored by rm, while quoted ones are expanded normally
rm cannot delete files with spaces unless the name is passed in double quotes twice
Double quotes disable globbing, which is the only thing that breaks names with spaces
Word splitting breaks unquoted expansions on whitespace. Quoting variables is the most important habit in safe shell use.
m
Redirection
What does the redirection 2>&1 do in a command such as cmd > out.log 2>&1?
Sends standard error to the same place as standard output
Sends standard output to the same place as standard error
Discards both output streams so nothing is written to the log
Runs the command twice and appends the second result to the file
File descriptor 2 (stderr) is duplicated onto descriptor 1 (stdout), which already points at out.log.
m
Pipes
In ps aux | grep sshd, what does the pipe do?
Feeds the standard output of ps into the standard input of grep
Runs ps and grep one after the other with no connection between them
Saves the output of ps to a file named grep in the current directory
Sends the output of grep back into ps to filter the process list
A pipe connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin, letting small tools be chained.
d
FHS key directories
Why is a new executable appearing in /tmp a common detection signal?
/tmp is world-writable, so attackers often stage tools there
/tmp is read-only, so only the kernel can create files in it
/tmp is where package managers install trusted system binaries
/tmp is excluded from file systems, so files there cannot run
/tmp is writable by every user and often cleared at reboot, which makes it a favoured staging area for intruders.
m
FHS key directories
Where does the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard place variable data such as logs and spool files?
/var
/usr
/boot
/opt
/var holds data that changes during operation: logs in /var/log, spools, caches and similar.
d
Inodes
What information does an inode hold, and what does it not hold?
Metadata such as owner, permissions, size and timestamps, but not the file's name
The file's name and path, but not its owner or permission bits
The file's contents in compressed form, but not its timestamps
The list of users who read the file, but not its size on disk
The inode stores metadata and block pointers. Names live in directory entries, which is why one inode can have several hard links.
d
Links
How does a symbolic link differ from a hard link?
A symbolic link stores a path and breaks if the target is removed; a hard link is another name for the same inode
A symbolic link copies the file's data; a hard link stores only the path to the original file
A symbolic link works only within one directory; a hard link works across different machines
A symbolic link needs root privileges; a hard link can be created only by the file's owner
A symlink points to a path and dangles if the target goes away. A hard link shares the inode, so the data stays until the last link is removed.
m
Everything is a file
What does the phrase 'everything is a file' mean on Linux?
Devices, processes and kernel data are exposed through file-like paths that tools can read
Every program must be stored as a single text file without any binary parts
All data on the system is stored in one large file inside the /root directory
The kernel converts every network packet into a file in the user's home directory
Devices appear under /dev, process data under /proc and kernel settings under /sys, so standard tools can work with them.
m
Paths
The current directory is /home/asha/reports. Which absolute path does ../logs/app.log refer to?
/home/asha/logs/app.log
/home/asha/reports/logs/app.log
/logs/app.log
/home/logs/app.log
.. moves up one level to /home/asha, so the relative path resolves to /home/asha/logs/app.log.
d
Path traversal
A web application builds a path as /srv/uploads/ + filename from user input. Why is a filename like ../../etc/passwd dangerous?
The .. components climb out of the intended directory to reach other files
The kernel refuses paths containing .. and crashes the web server process
The application will create a new directory called etc inside /srv/uploads
The filename is interpreted as a shell command and executed as root
Path traversal uses .. to escape a base directory. Applications must resolve and check the final path is still inside the allowed directory.
m
Reading ls -l
In the ls -l line -rw-r----- 1 asha finance 2048 report.csv, who can read the file?
The owner asha and members of the finance group
Everyone on the system, because the file is readable
Only asha, because the group has no permissions
Only members of finance, because the owner cannot read
rw- for the owner and r-- for the group give read access to asha and finance members; others have ---.
d
Deletion lifecycle
A large log file is deleted with rm while a running process still has it open. Why does disk usage not fall?
The inode and data stay allocated until the last open file handle is closed
rm only moves files to a hidden trash folder inside the user's home directory
The kernel keeps every deleted file for 24 hours in case it needs restoring
Disk usage figures are updated only after the next reboot of the system
Removing the name decrements the link count; space is freed only when no names and no open handles remain.
m
Safe deletion
Why is rm -rf with an unquoted variable, such as rm -rf $DIR/, risky in scripts?
If DIR is empty, the command becomes rm -rf / and targets the whole file system
If DIR is empty, rm refuses to run and the script stops with an error
rm -rf ignores variables and always deletes the current directory only
rm -rf asks for confirmation for every file, so scripts hang indefinitely
An empty or unset variable can turn the target into /. Quote variables and use safeguards such as ${DIR:?} in scripts.
d
Finding files
Which command finds files under /etc modified in the last day?
find /etc -type f -mtime -1
grep -r /etc --modified 1
ls -l /etc | sort -1
locate /etc -changed today
find's -mtime -1 matches files modified less than one day ago. grep searches content, not modification times.
m
grep
What does grep -i 'failed password' /var/log/auth.log do?
Prints lines containing the phrase, ignoring case
Counts how many users have failed passwords
Deletes lines with the phrase from the log
Prints only the lines that do not contain the phrase
-i makes the match case-insensitive. -v would invert it and -c would count matches.
d
Text toolchains
Which pipeline lists the ten source IPs that appear most often in a log where the IP is the first field?
cut -d' ' -f1 log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
sort log | head | cut -f1 | uniq -c
uniq -c log | cut -d' ' -f1 | head
head log | sort -rn | cut -f10 | uniq
Extract the field, sort so duplicates are adjacent, count with uniq -c, then sort numerically in reverse and take the top ten.
m
Documentation
Which command shows the manual page for the passwd configuration file rather than the passwd command?
man 5 passwd
man passwd --file
help passwd
info 1 passwd
Manual section 5 covers file formats; section 1 covers user commands.
d
Disk usage
df reports a file system 95% full, but du on its directories adds up to far less. What is a likely explanation?
Deleted files are still held open by running processes
du counts only hidden files, while df counts everything
df measures memory, not disk, so the figures differ
The file system is mounted read-only, which doubles usage
df reports allocated blocks, including space held by deleted-but-open files; du walks the names that still exist.
d
Identifying files
A file named invoice.pdf is reported as 'ELF 64-bit LSB executable' by the file command. What does this indicate?
The content is a Linux executable despite its extension, which deserves investigation
The PDF is corrupted and should be repaired with a document tool
The file command is wrong, because extensions define the file type
The file is a normal PDF compiled for 64-bit systems
file inspects content (magic bytes), not the name. A mismatch between name and content is a classic masquerading sign.

patch.echo itself searches the directory for f: echo itself searches the current directory for any files that match the pattern
